questions.question: Describe the contour patterns of a hill, a mountain, a ridge and a saddle, and explain how you would tell a hill from a depression.
questions.expected_answer: A hill: closed, roughly circular contours one inside another, highest in the centre, often with a trig station. A mountain: the same pattern but higher, steeper and with more closely spaced contours. A ridge: elongated closed contours along a long narrow crest. A saddle: a waisted or hourglass pattern between two sets of closed contours, the lowest point between two summits. A depression has inward ticks on its contours and heights that decrease towards the centre, whereas a hill's heights increase.

questions.question: Explain why valleys and spurs both form V-shaped contour patterns, and give three methods for telling them apart.
questions.expected_answer: A contour keeps one height. In a valley it runs upstream to where the river bed reaches that height, forming a V pointing uphill; around a spur it runs out around the tongue of high ground, forming a V pointing downhill. Methods: read the contour labels (heights increasing towards the point means valley, decreasing means spur); look for a river through the points of the V's (valley); look for spot heights on high ground within the V's (spur).

questions.question: Using the idea of a watershed and a saddle, explain how ridges influence drainage and the routes of roads.
questions.expected_answer: The crest of a ridge divides rain so that each side drains into a different valley and river; the ridge is a watershed between catchments. Ridges are barriers to movement, so roads follow valleys and cross the ridge at a saddle or nek, the lowest point between summits, often zigzagging up the approach to keep gradients gentle.
